Game: This is a picture, not a game: a triangle is cut into three pieces that turn into a rhombus. There is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and press the arrow keys. Move the slider to turn the pieces, and tick names or hint to see more.

Drag a corner, or focus it and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps). The slider turns the two pieces.

60°
Look for the math

A triangle is cut into three pieces and the pieces swing around two points. At the end the outline has four equal sides: a rhombus. The applet lets you drag the triangle, so you can find out when the trick works and when it does not.

Where the two cuts go

Let M be the midpoint of BC and Bm the midpoint of AC. The point N is where AB meets the circle centred at M with radius AB, so MN = AB. The cuts are MN and BmM. For N to lie on the segment AB, A must be outside that circle (AM > AB) while B is inside it (BM < AB). When there is no such N, the applet draws a dashed median AM and no pieces.

Two sides from a midline

Bm and M are midpoints of two sides of ABC, so BmM is parallel to AB and half as long: BmM = AB / 2. A half-turn about Bm sends M to M', and a half-turn about M sends N to N''. Since each half-turn moves a point by twice the distance to its centre, MM' = 2 × BmM = AB and N'N'' = 2 × BmM = AB. Notice that the length of N'N'' does not even depend on where N sits on AB.

Two sides from the cut

A rotation keeps every distance. Rotating N about M gives N'', so N''M = NM = AB. Rotating both M and N about Bm gives M' and N', so M'N' = MN = AB. At a 180° turn the four sides N'N'', N''M, MM' and M'N' therefore all equal AB, and the pieces tile that rhombus exactly. At other slider positions the outline is only part way through the turn.

What the hypotheses really say

The page quotes the olympiad problem with only AM > AB, then adds BM < AB when it describes the cut. That extra line matters: it does not follow from the olympiad hypothesis. Take a tall, thin acute triangle with angles near 89°, 89° and 2°: AM is much longer than AB, but BM is longer too, and its area is bigger than AB², so no rhombus of side AB could hold its pieces. Conversely, BM < AB alone can leave both A and B inside the circle. The logic test checked the rhombus claim on over 200 configurations where the cut exists (all four sides equal AB, to within 1e-9) and confirmed both failed implications; the applet shows the dashed median when the cut is impossible.

Try dragging C until the dashed median appears, then move it back and put the slider at 180°: the four sides of the rhombus reappear and stay equal to AB.
